unit.title: Plan and apply time management strategies

summary: This unit teaches you to plan your working time so that the right jobs are done well, safely and on time. You will learn to find out what must be done and by when, put tasks in order of priority, use simple planning tools, estimate how long jobs take and work with the clock, deal with time wasters and interruptions, work with others to meet deadlines, look after your health and workload, and review how you use your time so that you plan better next time.

blocks.p: This unit is shared by the Welding Level 2 and Hospitality (villa and property services) Level 2 programmes, so its examples come from a fabrication shop, a villa and other workplaces. **Time management** means planning and controlling how you use your working time, so that the right jobs are done well and on time.

Good time management is not rushing. It is knowing what must be done, choosing what to do first, judging how long each job takes, keeping to the plan, and changing the plan sensibly when something goes wrong. A welder who promises a gate for Friday and delivers it on Friday, and a housekeeper whose rooms are ready before the guests arrive, are both managing their time.

head: What you must be able to do
What this means at work
rows: Find out what must be done
Get your tasks and deadlines from the supervisor, job sheets, work orders, rosters and guest lists; ask when anything is unclear.
Sort tasks by how urgent and how important they are, with safety first.
Use to-do lists, checklists, routines, calendars, rosters, work schedules and Gantt charts.
Break jobs into steps and include set-up, checks, clean-up and some extra time.
Use 12-hour and 24-hour times, add up times, and work back from a deadline.
Spot what wastes time, deal politely with interruptions, and re-plan.
Share machines and tasks, delegate, and tell people early about delays.
Take breaks, drink water, rest, and notice the signs of too heavy a workload.
Keep a time log, compare the plan with what happened, and set SMART goals.

ul: A **multiple-choice theory paper** on why time matters, deadlines, priorities, planning tools, estimating, time wasters, interruptions, teamwork, goals and reviewing.
A **written paper** with short answers (trade terms, 24-hour times, simple time sums) and longer answers in full sentences.

**Two group practicals.** In the first, your group plans a Monday-to-Friday schedule for a team from a scenario card (a fabrication shop or a villa): every task on a sticky note, sorted on an urgent and important grid, with time estimates and a schedule or Gantt chart, presented to the assessor. In the second, you work through a planned day while the assessor hands out interruption cards; you re-plan, tell the "supervisor" or "customer" about changes, keep a time log, and fill in a review sheet.

blocks.note: In every plan, PPE, safety checks, maintenance, breaks and clean-up stay in. Planning them out to save time is a mistake that assessors look for.
blocks.label: Remember

head: Who gains
How good time management helps
rows: Less stress and less rushing at the end of the day
Fewer mistakes, so less work to redo
A good name, which leads to more responsibility and better pay
Work starts as planned, so nobody is held up waiting for you
Shared machines, tools and staff are used well
Jobs finished on time keep customers and bring repeat work
Less wasted labour and materials, so lower costs
The gate is fitted on the day promised
The villa is clean and ready before check-in

ul: Often late, or rushing at the end of the shift.
Missed deadlines and forgotten tasks.
Jobs done twice because they were rushed the first time.
Time lost searching for tools and materials.
Working through breaks and staying late most days.
Safety checks skipped "to save time".

blocks.p: **Punctuality** means arriving at work, at meetings and at customers' homes on time. When you are late, the team cannot start as planned, a shared job is held up, and a customer or guest is left waiting.

To be on time, work back from your start time. Example: your shift starts at 07:30. You need 10 minutes to change and get to your bay, and 15 minutes to walk from the bus stop, and the bus ride takes 40 minutes. 07:30 − 10 minutes = 07:20; − 15 minutes = 07:05; − 40 minutes = **06:25**. Catch that bus or an earlier one.

blocks.note: Traffic, rain and route taxis that leave only when full can all make you late. Plan to arrive 10 to 15 minutes early. If you will be late, call or message your supervisor before your start time, not after it.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.p: Before you can plan, you need the full list of tasks and their deadlines. A **deadline** is the time or date by which a job must be done. Get your tasks from the right place, and if you are not given a deadline, ask for one.

head: Where it comes from
What it tells you
rows: The jobs for today, the order to do them in, and any special points
Job sheet, job card or work order
What the customer wants, sizes, materials and the date it is due
Who works which shift and which days
Check-out and check-in times, number of guests, special requests
Which clients come at what time, for which service
The short meeting at the start of a shift where the team hears about the day's work and safety

blocks.note: When a supervisor gives you several jobs at once, write them down with their deadlines. It is easy to forget one job, or one detail, in a busy day.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: A **routine** is a regular, set order of tasks that you follow every day, such as the checks at the start of a shift. A **checklist** is a written list of checks or steps that you tick off, so that nothing is missed. Both save time: you do not have to work out the steps from scratch each time, and you do not have to go back for something forgotten.

head: Fabrication shop: start of shift
Villa: room turnover
rows: Strip the beds; collect used linen and towels
Empty the bins; check for guests' belongings left behind
Gas hoses and regulators checked for leaks
Clean the bathroom: shower, toilet, basin, mirror, floor
Extraction on; fire extinguisher in place
Make the beds; put out fresh towels and amenities
Drawings and job cards for the day collected
Dust, then sweep or vacuum and mop; check lights, air conditioning and remote control
Final check against the room checklist; report any damage

blocks.p: To **prioritise** is to put tasks in order of how much they matter. Ask two questions about each task. Is it **urgent**: must it be done soon? Is it **important**: does it matter a lot for safety, for customers or for the business? The answers place each task in one of four boxes of a priority grid.

head: Box
What to do
Workshop examples
Villa examples
rows: A smell of gas in the workshop
A customer's cracked handrail that people are using
A guest locked out of a room
A room needed for check-in within the hour
Plan a set time for it, before it becomes urgent
Ordering consumables before they run out
A deep clean of the kitchen
Deal with it quickly, or pass it to the right person
A sales caller who wants an answer today
A routine form someone wants back by lunch
A delivery driver asking for directions
Do it last, or drop it
Sorting old magazines in the staff room
Re-arranging posters on the notice board
Re-arranging the store shelves for looks

blocks.note: Many people spend their day in boxes 3 and 4, and the box 2 jobs turn into emergencies. Planning box 2 jobs (maintenance, ordering, training) before they become urgent is the heart of good time management.
blocks.label: Tip

ol: Anything that is a danger to people: make it safe and report it.
Jobs due soonest, and jobs that other people are waiting for.
Jobs that need a shared machine or person, at the time it is free.
Important jobs that are not yet urgent, at a time you have planned.

blocks.note: Safety checks are never cut to catch up time. Checking a gas hose, a lifting sling, a ladder or a cable takes minutes; an accident costs days, money and sometimes a life.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.p: If two jobs are due at the same time and you cannot do both, or a new job arrives on a day that is already full, tell your supervisor **early**. Explain what else you have, and agree which job comes first. Do not quietly drop one job, rush in an unsafe way, or refuse rudely.

head: Tool
What it is
Best for
Watch out for
rows: A list of tasks, often in priority order
One person's jobs for the day; tick each off when done
Shows no times and no names
A list of steps or checks to tick
Only as good as the list: keep it up to date
Days and dates with fixed events
Meetings, deliveries, guest arrivals, days off and deadlines over weeks or months
A chart of who works which shift
A table of which tasks are done, by whom and when
Must be changed when plans change
Each task drawn as a bar along a timeline
Bigger jobs with steps that follow each other; seeing at a glance whether a job is on time
Takes longer to draw and update
Only useful if you act on them, and keep the phone for work use

blocks.p: This Gantt chart plans a steel stair rail for a house, from measuring to fitting, over one week. Read along each row to see when a task starts and ends.

head: Task
Mon
Tue
Wed
Thu
Fri
rows: Measure on site; confirm the drawing
Fit on site; customer checks and accepts

blocks.p: A **milestone** is a key point that marks the end of a main stage, such as "frame welded" or "rail fitted and accepted". The chart shows that painting cannot start until welding ends, so if welding runs a day late, every later task, and the handover, moves too unless something is changed.

Plan tomorrow at the end of today: check what is done, what is left and what is due, and write tomorrow's list before you go home. Five minutes of planning in the afternoon saves much more the next morning, and you start the day knowing exactly what to do.

sections.title: Estimating time and working with the clock

blocks.h: Estimating how long a job takes

flow: Break the job into steps
Estimate each step from your own records, or ask your supervisor
Include the "hidden" time: fetching materials, setting up, putting on PPE, safety checks, checking the work, drying or curing, and cleaning up
Add the steps together
Add some extra time for delays such as a power cut or a busy machine (often about 10 to 15%)
Write the estimate down; afterwards compare it with the real time and use what you learn next time

head: Example: making a small steel gate frame
Time
rows: Read the drawing, list and collect the materials
Clean, fit up and tack; check it is square
Clean up the bay and put the tools back

blocks.note: When a job takes longer than you planned, do not just promise to work faster next time. Find out which step took longer and why, and plan more time for that step next time.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: Job cards, rosters and guest lists often use the 24-hour clock. It runs from 00:00 (midnight) to 23:59, so there is no need for a.m. or p.m.

ul: For a p.m. time from 1:00 p.m. onwards, add 12 to the hour: 4:10 p.m. becomes 16:10.
For an a.m. time, keep the hour and write it with two digits: 8:05 a.m. becomes 08:05.
To change back, take 12 away from hours 13 to 23 and write p.m.: 21:30 becomes 9:30 p.m.

blocks.p: There are **60 minutes in an hour**, not 100. Add the hours first, then the minutes; when the minutes reach 60 or more, change 60 minutes into 1 hour. Example: a job starts at 09:50 and takes 2 hours 25 minutes. 09:50 + 2 hours = 11:50; + 25 minutes = 12:15.

ul: 2.5 hours = 2 hours 30 minutes = 150 minutes.
1.25 hours = 1 hour 15 minutes; 45 minutes = 0.75 hours.
Hours worked: 08:00 to 16:30 is 8 hours 30 minutes; take away a 1-hour lunch and 7 hours 30 minutes are worked.

blocks.p: To find the latest time you can start, count back from the deadline. Example: three rooms must be ready by 15:00. Each takes 50 minutes, and the final check takes 20 minutes: 3 × 50 + 20 = 170 minutes = 2 hours 50 minutes. The latest start is 15:00 − 2 hours 50 minutes = **12:10**. Start earlier than that, to leave room for delays.
The same works with days. A job that needs 4 full working days and must be finished by the end of Thursday has to start by Monday morning at the latest (Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday).

head: Time waster
How to reduce it
rows: Tidy, labelled storage; a shadow board for tools; put each tool back after use
Personal calls, messages and social media
Keep your phone in your locker or bag and use it on breaks, unless there is an emergency
Say politely that you are busy and offer to talk at the break
**Procrastination**: putting off a task you should do now
Break it into small steps; start with a short, fixed time such as 10 minutes; do it early in the day
Redoing work because the instructions were not clear
Ask questions; read the drawing or job sheet; check measurements before you cut
Waiting for machines, materials or people
Book shared machines; order stock early; do other work while you wait
**Multitasking**: trying to do two or more tasks at the same time
Do one task at a time; finish it, then move on
List the tasks, set priorities and estimate times before you start

blocks.p: Multitasking feels busy but wastes time. Every switch between jobs means getting back into the work, and mistakes creep in. Near machines, splitting your attention is also dangerous.

blocks.note: Checking your phone every few minutes breaks your concentration. Each time, it takes a while to get back into the job, the work takes longer, and there are more mistakes.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: **Planned** interruptions are known in advance: the morning meeting, lunch, a weekly cleaning task on the roster. Put them in your plan. **Unplanned** interruptions are not: a machine breaks down, steel is delivered late, a worker calls in sick, a guest checks in early, a customer wants a job sooner. **Downtime** is time when a machine or a worker cannot work, because of a breakdown or while waiting for materials.

flow: Stay calm and find out the facts
Make anything unsafe safe, and report a breakdown
Decide the new priorities: what must still be done today?
Change the plan: move tasks, swap their order, use waiting time for other work
Tell the people affected (supervisor, team, customer or guest) early, with a new time
Note the cause, so that it can be planned for next time

blocks.p: You can protect your time without being rude. To a co-worker who wants to chat: "I need to finish this report by eleven. Can we talk at lunch?" To a request you cannot fit in: "I'm on the canopy job until three. Shall I ask the supervisor which one should come first?"
Teamwork saves time when tasks are shared out clearly, people help each other, and nobody does the same job twice. Everyone needs to know what the others are doing and when.

ul: **Share machines and tools fairly.** Agree or book a time for a shared bandsaw, grinder, ladder or vehicle, and do other work until it is free. Never take one while its user is away.

**Delegation** means handing a task to another suitable person to do, while you stay responsible for it being done. Give clear instructions and a deadline, check that the person is trained and allowed to do it, and check on progress.
**Rosters** show who is working when. Check yours, swap shifts only through your supervisor, and plan around days off.
**Meetings** save time when they are short and planned. An **agenda**, the list of points to be discussed, sent out before the meeting, keeps everyone to the point.
**Toolbox talks** at the start of a shift make sure everyone knows the day's work and its hazards.

blocks.h: When you cannot meet a deadline

flow: Tell your supervisor as soon as you know the job will be late, not after the deadline has passed
Explain the reason honestly, how much is done and how much is left
Give a realistic new time
Suggest solutions: help from a co-worker, a change in the order of work, finishing the most important part first
Never skip safety or quality checks to catch up
If the supervisor agrees, tell the customer or guest politely, with the new time
Note the cause, so that it can be planned for next time

blocks.note: Customers plan around the dates you give them. A delay they hear about early, with a reason and a new time, is far easier for them to accept than a surprise on the day.
blocks.label: Tip

sections.title: Your health, your workload and reviewing your time

blocks.p: A tired worker works slowly and makes more mistakes, and mistakes take time to fix. In welding and machine work, tiredness also makes accidents more likely, and an accident costs far more time than a break. Short planned breaks, drinking water and eating properly keep your energy up, especially in a hot workshop or when cleaning villa after villa in the summer heat. Enough sleep means you arrive on time and alert.

blocks.h: Signs that a workload is too heavy

ul: Always working through breaks and often staying late.
Missing deadlines, or forgetting tasks.
Making more mistakes than usual.
Feeling stressed, unable to sleep, getting headaches.
Being short-tempered with co-workers or customers.

blocks.p: If you see these signs, re-plan and re-prioritise, ask for help, and talk to your supervisor about your workload **before** it causes harm.
A **time log** is a record of what you did and how long it took. It shows how you really spend your time, which is often different from what you think.

head: Time
What I was doing
Notes
rows: Looking for the big grinder and a cutting disc
Time waster: not put back yesterday
Cutting tubes for the canopy frame
Fitting and tacking the canopy frame

flow: Record honestly every 30 minutes, or each time you change task, including breaks, interruptions and phone use
At the end of the week, add up the time spent on each kind of activity
Compare it with your plan
Find the biggest time wasters
Choose two or three changes
Try them the next week, check again, and talk about the results with your supervisor

blocks.p: A goal for better time management should be **SMART**: specific, measurable, achievable, relevant and time-bound. "I will be quicker" is not SMART. These are:

ul: "By the end of this month I will cut, fit and tack a standard gate frame in 90 minutes or less, checked by my supervisor."
"From Monday I will turn over a standard double room to the checklist in 40 minutes, and record my times for two weeks."
"Next week I will cut my time spent looking for tools to under one hour, measured by my time log."

blocks.note: Reviewing your time is part of continuous improvement: plan, do the work, check what really happened, and change the plan. Each week you plan a little better.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: Use this checklist to test yourself. If you cannot honestly say "I can" to a line, go back to that section and practise it.

ul: I can explain why good time management matters to me, my team, the business and its customers.
I can say where to find my tasks and deadlines, and I ask when a deadline is not clear.
I can use routines and checklists so that nothing is forgotten.
I can sort tasks on an urgent and important grid and say what to do with each box.
I can explain why safety checks and maintenance are never cut to save time.
I can say what to do when two jobs clash or a new job arrives on a full day.
I can choose between a to-do list, a calendar, a roster, a work schedule and a Gantt chart.
I can read a simple Gantt chart and explain what a milestone is.
I can estimate the time for a job, including set-up, checks, clean-up and extra time.
I can change between 12-hour and 24-hour times and add or take away times correctly.
I can work back from a deadline to find the latest start time.
I can name common time wasters, including procrastination and multitasking, and say how to reduce each.
I can deal with planned and unplanned interruptions and re-plan calmly.
I can share machines, delegate a task and take part in short, planned meetings.
I can say what to do when I cannot meet a deadline.
I can name signs of too heavy a workload and say what to do.
I can keep a time log and use it to improve, and set SMART goals for my time.

terms: Agenda
The list of points to be discussed at a meeting, sent out before it starts
Checklist
A written list of checks or steps that you tick so that nothing is missed

Delegation
Handing a task to another suitable person while you stay responsible for it being done

Gantt chart
A chart that shows each task as a bar along a timeline

Something that stops your planned work; planned (known in advance) or unplanned

Multitasking
Trying to do two or more tasks at the same time

Put tasks in order of how much they matter
Procrastination
Putting off a task that you should do now
Punctuality

Routine

A board with the outline of each tool painted on it, so tools are put back in place and a missing one shows
SMART goal
A goal that is specific, measurable, achievable, relevant and time-bound
Time log
A record of what you did and how long it took
To-do list
A list of tasks you need to do, often in priority order

A short meeting at the start of a shift about the day's work and safety
Urgent task
A task that must be done soon
Work schedule
A plan showing which tasks are done, by whom and when
24-hour clock
A way of writing times from 00:00 to 23:59, with no a.m. or p.m.

c1.title: Monday at a fabrication shop in Hayes
c1.text: Javaughn works at a small fabrication shop in Hayes, Clarendon. At 07:30 on Monday his supervisor, Mr Lindo, gives him these jobs: steel stair rails for a house, due on Wednesday; a clinic's water-tank stand with a broken leg, reported this morning as leaning; ordering welding rods and grinding discs, which will run out on Thursday; the monthly check of the shop's two welding machines, due by Friday; and tidying the scrap corner before a collection next week. The shop has one bandsaw, which another welder has booked from 08:00 to 10:00.

c2.title: Changeover day at a villa in Discovery Bay
c2.text: Petagaye is a housekeeper at a five-bedroom villa in Discovery Bay, St Ann. Today the departing guests check out at 11:00 and a new family checks in at 15:00. Each bedroom with its bathroom takes her about 35 minutes to turn over, and the kitchen and living areas take 1 hour 10 minutes. The villa manager, Mrs Rowe, wants 20 minutes for a final walk-through before the guests arrive. A second housekeeper, Lorna, starts work at 12:00.

c3.title: A late steel delivery in Ewarton
c3.text: Damion is making a steel canopy frame for a church in Ewarton, St Catherine, and has promised it for Saturday morning. On Wednesday at 10:00 the supplier phones: the 50 mm square tube will now arrive on Friday afternoon instead of Wednesday afternoon. Once the tube arrives, Damion needs two full days to cut, weld and paint the frame. The base plates, brackets and fixing bolts are already in the shop.

c4.title: A trainee's time log in Christiana
c4.text: Shanoya, a welding trainee on work experience at a steel shop in Christiana, Manchester, kept a time log for one 40-hour week. She logged 26 hours welding, cutting and fitting; 4 hours looking for tools, clamps and discs; 3 hours waiting for the shared grinder; 2 hours on personal phone messages; 2.5 hours in meetings and toolbox talks; and 2.5 hours cleaning up. She also noted that while tacking she kept stopping to answer the shop phone and check the electrode oven.

c5.title: A new maintenance job in Falmouth
c5.text: Tevin has started work in the maintenance department of a hotel in Falmouth, Trelawny. His shift starts at 06:30, and the route taxi from his district often leaves late; he has been 20 minutes late twice this week. His work order says a pump contractor will arrive at 13:45 and that Tevin must meet him with the pump-room key. By his third week, Tevin is working through his lunch break most days, staying late, and has started forgetting small jobs.

questions.q: Which of Javaughn's jobs belongs in the "urgent and important" box?
o: Ordering rods and discs before Thursday
Making the clinic's leaning tank stand safe
The monthly check of the welding machines
Tidying the scrap corner for collection
questions.why: A leaning tank stand full of water could collapse and hurt someone, so it is both urgent and important. The order and the machine check are important but not yet urgent, so they get a planned time; the scrap corner can wait.

questions.q: Where should the consumables order go in Javaughn's plan?
o: Thursday morning, when the rods and discs actually run out
Nowhere: Mr Lindo will notice when stock is low and order it
At a set time early in the week, before it becomes urgent
First thing on Monday, ahead of the leaning tank stand
questions.why: The order is important but not urgent. Ordering on the day the stock runs out leaves the shop waiting with no rods, so plan it early in the week; the safety job still comes before it.

questions.q: Javaughn needs the bandsaw to cut the stair-rail parts. What is the best plan for 08:00 to 10:00?
o: Do work that needs no bandsaw, and book it for 10:00
Use the bandsaw while the other welder is on his tea break
Wait beside the bandsaw so that he does not lose his turn
Ask Mr Lindo to cancel the other welder's booking for him
questions.why: Shared machines are booked so that work does not clash. Using the waiting time for other tasks, such as the tank stand or the order, means no time is lost; taking a machine while its user is away causes conflict and can be unsafe.

questions.q: Javaughn plans the stair rails as 5 hours of cutting and welding. Mr Lindo says the estimate is too short. What has Javaughn most likely left out?
o: The time the house owner will need to pay for the rails
Fetching steel, set-up, checking, priming and clean-up
The time other welders will spend on their own jobs
The time it takes to write his to-do list each morning
questions.why: An estimate must include the hidden time around the main work: collecting materials, setting up, checking, finishing and cleaning up, plus a little extra for delays. Leaving these out is the most common reason jobs run late.

questions.q: Working alone, how long would Petagaye need for the whole changeover, including the walk-through?
o: 4 hours 05 minutes
4 hours 40 minutes
3 hours 15 minutes
4 hours 25 minutes
questions.why: Bedrooms: 5 × 35 = 175 minutes. Add 70 minutes for the kitchen and living areas and 20 minutes for the walk-through: 265 minutes. 265 ÷ 60 = 4 remainder 25, so 4 hours 25 minutes: more than the 4 hours between check-out and check-in.

questions.q: What should Petagaye do about the time shortfall?
o: Tell Mrs Rowe now and agree which rooms Lorna takes at 12:00
Skip the walk-through, as the guests will check the rooms
Work faster and leave the bathrooms until the next morning
Wait until 14:30 to see whether she is really running late
questions.why: A problem seen early can be planned for: with Lorna starting at 12:00 there is enough time if the work is shared out. Leaving out checks or parts of the job, or waiting until it is too late, leads to unhappy guests.

questions.q: At 12:40 Mrs Rowe phones: the new family's flight landed early and they will arrive at 14:00. What should Petagaye do?
o: Carry on with the plan, since 15:00 was the agreed check-in time
Agree with Mrs Rowe which areas must be ready by 14:00, and re-plan
Leave the rooms half done and wait at the gate to greet the family
Finish the remaining rooms in half the time by missing the checklist
questions.why: An unplanned change means re-planning, not panicking. Agree the new priorities with the manager, get ready first the areas the guests will see and use first, and keep the checklist so that standards do not drop.

questions.q: Petagaye uses the same turnover checklist for every bedroom. How does this save her time?
o: She can skip rooms that looked clean when the guests left
The manager no longer needs to do a final walk-through
Nothing is forgotten, so she does not have to go back
It lets her clean two rooms at once without mistakes
questions.why: A checklist means she does not have to work out the steps each time and nothing is missed, so she does not have to return to a room for a forgotten towel or an unemptied bin. The manager's check is still needed.

questions.q: What should Damion do first?
o: Say nothing until Friday, in case the tube comes early after all
Plan to work all of Friday night, without breaks, to catch up
Tell the church on Saturday morning that the frame is not ready
Tell his supervisor today, with the reason and his options
questions.why: Delays are reported as soon as they are known, not when the deadline arrives. On Wednesday there is still time to look for tube elsewhere, re-plan the work or agree a new date with the church.

questions.q: Which of these would help Damion stay as close as possible to his deadline without cutting corners?
o: Prepare the base plates, brackets and paint area while he waits
Use thinner tube from the offcut rack so that he can start today
Leave out the primer, since the frame will be under a roof
Skip the squareness check, as the frame will be bolted in place
questions.why: Doing the parts of the job that do not need the tube turns waiting time into useful time. Changing the material or leaving out primer or checks lowers quality and safety, and the frame may have to be made again.

questions.q: Damion's supervisor agrees a new handover time of Monday at 14:00. How should the church be told?
o: Only if the church secretary phones to ask about the frame
Politely and straight away, with the reason and the new time
By a message on Saturday morning, so as not to worry them early
With a discount offer, but without giving them a new date
questions.why: Customers plan around your dates, so tell them early, honestly and with a realistic new time; this keeps their trust. Then note the cause, a late supply, so that steel is ordered with more time in hand next time.

questions.q: Which change would save Shanoya the most time next week?
o: Keeping her phone in her bag during working time
Leaving out the toolbox talks so she can start sooner
A shadow board and fixed places for tools and clamps
Doing less cleaning up at the end of each day
questions.why: Searching for tools cost her 4 hours, the biggest loss in her log; a shadow board and fixed places cut most of it. Phone use (2 hours) is worth fixing too, but toolbox talks and clean-up are part of safe work, not time wasters.

questions.q: Why does stopping to answer the phone and check the oven while tacking slow Shanoya down?
o: Each switch breaks her concentration and lets mistakes in
The phone and the oven draw power that the welder needs
Tacking goes faster when it is done in short, quick bursts
Answering the shop phone is never part of a trainee's job
questions.why: Multitasking means stopping, then getting back into the job each time, so the work takes longer and errors in fit-up are more likely. Agree who answers the phone, and check the oven at set times.

questions.q: Which goal for next week is SMART?
o: "I will try much harder to stop wasting time at work."
"I will be the most organised trainee in the whole shop."
"I will waste a lot less time from now on, starting soon."
"Next week I will search for tools for under 1 hour in all."
questions.why: It is specific (time spent searching), measurable (under 1 hour, checked in her next time log), achievable with a shadow board, relevant to her biggest time waster and time-bound (next week). The others give no number and no deadline.

questions.q: At the end of the week, what should Shanoya do with her time log?
o: Hand it in and keep the same plan, as one week proves nothing
Compare it with her plan, choose two changes and try them
Throw it away, since last week is over and cannot be changed
Show it to her friends to prove how hard she worked all week
questions.why: A time log is useful only when it is reviewed: compare it with the plan, pick out the biggest wastes, choose a few changes, try them and check again. Talking it over with her supervisor helps too.

questions.q: What is the best way for Tevin to stop arriving late?
o: Explain to his supervisor each time that the taxi was late
Make up the lost time by skipping his start-of-shift checks
Take an earlier taxi, aiming to arrive 10–15 minutes early
Ask a co-worker to sign him in on days he is running late
questions.why: Punctuality is planned: if a route is unreliable, leave earlier so that a late taxi does not make you late. Excuses do not fix the problem, skipping checks is unsafe, and getting someone to sign you in is dishonest.

questions.q: Tevin writes in his phone diary: "Pump contractor 3:45". What will happen if he goes by his diary?
o: He will be on time, as 13:45 and 3:45 are the same
He will be two hours late, as 13:45 is 1:45 p.m.
He will be an hour early, as 13:45 is 2:45 p.m.
He will be two hours early, as 13:45 is 5:45 p.m.
questions.why: To change a 24-hour time after noon, take away 12: 13:45 − 12 = 1:45 p.m. Arriving at 3:45 p.m., he would keep the contractor waiting two hours with no key.

questions.q: What should Tevin do about working through lunch, staying late and forgetting jobs?
o: Talk to his supervisor about his workload and re-plan priorities
Keep going, since tiredness is normal in the first months of a job
Drink energy drinks so that he can work through all his breaks
Quietly leave some jobs off his list without telling anyone
questions.why: These are signs of a workload that is too heavy. Tired workers are slower, make more mistakes and have more accidents, so he should take his breaks, re-plan and talk to his supervisor early.

questions.q: On a Gantt chart for a gate, "weld out" runs from Tuesday to Thursday morning and "paint" from Thursday afternoon to Friday. The welding is now a day behind. What does the chart tell the planner?
o: Painting can still start on time, as it is on its own row
Only the welding bar needs moving, as the end date is fixed
Painting must also move a day later, so handover may slip
The chart has failed and should be swapped for a to-do list
questions.why: A Gantt chart shows that painting cannot start until welding ends. When welding slips, every later task moves too unless the planner adds help or changes the order, so the customer may need to be told.

questions.q: A supervisor delegates the weekly check of the fire extinguishers to a trained trainee. Who is responsible for making sure the check is done?
o: Only the trainee, once the task has been handed over
Nobody, as a weekly check is only a suggestion
The firm that services the extinguishers each year
The supervisor, who should check that it was done
questions.why: Delegation hands over the doing, not the responsibility. The supervisor gives clear instructions and a deadline, and then checks that the task was done properly.
